title: Both agree: the act cannot be separated from God's motion, yet a power to cease or to the opposite remains
source_text: XXI. Utrique ergo in eo conveniunt, necesse esse ut agat ille quem ad agendum movet atque impellit divinae gratiae, vel providentiae vis & efficacia, & rationis propriae dictamen, quoniam ab illa motione Dei & judicii proprii determinatione actio hominis separari non potest: & tamen cum ejusmodi actu, adeoque cum motione Dei ad talem actum consistere potestatem ad cessationem ab illo, aut etiam ad actum oppositum, qua ratione saepius expositum & repetitum est.
pass_a_gloss: Both therefore agree in this, that it is necessary that he act whom the force and efficacy of divine grace, or of providence, and the dictate of his own reason move and impel to acting, since from that motion of God and determination of his own judgment the action of man cannot be separated: and yet that with an act of that kind, and so with the motion of God to such an act, consists the power to cessation from it, or also to the opposite act, in the manner which has been oftener set forth and repeated.
pass_b_english: Both sides, then, agree on two points. A man whom the force and efficacy of God's grace or providence, together with his own reason's dictate, moves and drives to act must act, because his action cannot be separated from that motion of God and that determination of his own judgment.
And yet with such an act, and so with God's motion toward it, there coexists a power to stop it or even to do the opposite, in the way that has been explained and repeated more than once.

choices.why: Kept as the technical phrase both Reformed parties use; it marks the necessity that removes the power to act otherwise, as against a necessity of infallibility.
